```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE)
library(permutest)
```

## Overview

`permutest` runs permutation (randomization) tests for any test statistic and
any randomization scheme, and builds confidence intervals by inverting those
tests, following Glazer and Stark (2024). This vignette describes the development
version, which adds `npc_many()` and revises `npc()`: a per-outcome shift (or one
value used for every outcome) and an `alternative` argument that applies to every
outcome.

Everything is built around one generic function, `permutation_test()`. It takes
a data frame and two plug-ins:

* `test_stat`: how to summarise the data (difference in means, a t statistic,
  or any function you write);
* `perm_func`: how to re-randomise the group labels (shuffle them, shuffle
  within strata, flip signs), or a matrix of relabellings supplied as
  `perm_set`.

The other functions are layers on top of it.

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `two_sample()`, `one_sample()` | Shortcuts for the difference in means and the one-sample mean |
| `permutation_test_ci()` | Confidence interval by inverting the test |
| `npc()` | Combines tests on several outcomes (nonparametric combination) |
| `npc_many()` | `npc()` over a grid of shifts, with one shared set of relabellings |
| `tippett()`, `fisher()`, `liptak()` | Combining functions used by `npc()` |
| `adjust_p_value()` | Holm-Bonferroni, Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustments |

## A first test

The data are two samples, `x` (treatment) and `y` (control).

```{r data}
x <- c(35.3, 35.9, 37.2, 33.0, 31.9, 33.7, 36.0, 35.0,
       33.3, 33.6, 37.9, 35.6, 29.0, 33.7, 35.7)
y <- c(32.5, 34.0, 34.4, 31.8, 35.0, 34.6, 33.5, 33.6,
       31.5, 33.8, 34.6)

two_sample(x, y, alternative = "greater", reps = 10^4, seed = 42)
```

The result is a p-value for the null hypothesis that treatment had no effect,
against the alternative that it increased the outcome. `alternative` can be
`"greater"`, `"less"` or `"two-sided"`.

## The generic test

`two_sample()` wraps `permutation_test()`, which takes a data frame and the
names of its columns.

```{r generic}
df <- data.frame(group   = c(rep(1, length(x)), rep(0, length(y))),
                 outcome = c(x, y))

out <- permutation_test(df, group_col = "group", outcome_col = "outcome",
                        test_stat = "diff_in_means",
                        perm_func = permute_group,
                        alternative = "greater",
                        shift = 0,
                        reps = 10^4,
                        return_test_dist = TRUE,
                        return_perm_dist = TRUE,
                        seed = 42)
out$p_value
```

Three conventions to know:

* **The treatment group is the first value of `group_col` to appear in the
  data.** Here that is `1`, because the treated rows come first. If the control
  rows came first the sign of the statistic would flip. The function warns
  about the choice ("... being used as value for treatment"); warnings are
  switched off in this vignette.
* **The p-value counts the observed labelling.** For sampled permutations it is
  (number of permuted statistics at least as large as the observed one, plus
  one) divided by (`reps` plus one). With `complete_enum = TRUE` it is the plain
  fraction.
* **The output** is a list: `p_value`, `test_stat_dist` (the permutation
  distribution, if requested) and `perm_indices_mat` (one relabelling per row,
  if requested).

```{r dist, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
hist(out$test_stat_dist, breaks = 40, main = "Permutation distribution",
     xlab = "Difference in means")
abline(v = diff_in_means(df, "group", "outcome", treatment_value = 1),
       col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

### Testing a non-zero effect

`shift` tests the hypothesis that treatment added a constant to every treated
unit. Units that change group under a relabelling are adjusted by the shift.

```{r shift}
permutation_test(df, "group", "outcome", alternative = "two-sided",
                 shift = 2, reps = 10^4, seed = 42)$p_value
```

The set of shifts that are not rejected at level $\alpha$ is a confidence set.
`permutation_test_ci()` computes it for one outcome, as shown below.

## Plugging in a test statistic

`test_stat` is either a string (`"diff_in_means"`, `"diff_in_medians"`,
`"mean"`) or a function of `(df, group_col, outcome_col)` that returns one
number. Larger values should mean more evidence for the "greater" alternative.

```{r custom-stat}
trimmed_diff <- function(df, group_col, outcome_col) {
  treated <- df[[group_col]] == 1       # fix the treatment label explicitly
  mean(df[[outcome_col]][treated], trim = 0.1) -
    mean(df[[outcome_col]][!treated], trim = 0.1)
}

permutation_test(df, "group", "outcome", test_stat = trimmed_diff,
                 alternative = "two-sided", reps = 5000, seed = 1)$p_value
```

Write the treatment label into the function, as above. A statistic that works
out the treatment group from the data it is given can change orientation on a
permuted data frame.

## Plugging in a permutation scheme

`perm_func` takes `(df, group_col, strata_col, seed)` and returns the data frame
with the group column rearranged.

```{r strata}
df$stratum <- c(rep(1:2, length.out = length(x)),
                rep(1:2, length.out = length(y)))

permutation_test(df, "group", "outcome", strata_col = "stratum",
                 perm_func = strat_permute_group,
                 alternative = "greater", reps = 5000, seed = 1)$p_value
```

`permute_sign` flips signs for the one-sample problem, and `one_sample()` uses
it.

### Reusing relabellings, and complete enumeration

You can pass your own matrix of relabellings in `perm_set`, one row per
relabelling. Reusing one set across many tests is the idea behind the fast
confidence-interval algorithm: coverage depends only on the test at the true
value, so one Monte Carlo sample serves every hypothesised shift.

When the number of assignments is small, you can enumerate all of them and ask
for the exact p-value.

```{r enum}
small <- data.frame(group   = c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0),
                    outcome = c(5.1, 6.3, 4.8, 3.9, 4.4, 5.0))

all_assignments <- t(combn(6, 3, function(i) {
  g <- rep(0, 6); g[i] <- 1; g
}))
dim(all_assignments)

permutation_test(small, "group", "outcome", alternative = "greater",
                 perm_set = all_assignments, complete_enum = TRUE)$p_value
```

## Confidence intervals for one outcome

`permutation_test_ci()` inverts the two-sided test by bisection and returns the
observed statistic and the interval.

```{r ci}
ci <- permutation_test_ci(df, "group", "outcome",
                          test_stat = "diff_in_means",
                          perm_func = permute_group,
                          cl = 0.95, e = 0.01, reps = 10^4, seed = 42)
ci$obs_diff
ci$ci
```

* `cl` is the confidence level; `e` is how close the bisection has to get to
  each endpoint, so a smaller `e` takes more steps.
* The relabellings are generated once and reused at every shift.
* For `"diff_in_means"` (and `"mean"` in the one-sample problem) the statistic
  at a new shift is computed from the one at shift 0, using the number of
  treated units each relabelling moves to control. Other statistics re-run
  `permutation_test()` at every shift, which is much slower.
* Leave `upper_bracket` and `lower_bracket` as `NULL`. The function checks that
  its starting brackets contain the endpoints and stops with an error if they
  do not.
* The interval is for a constant shift. It remains valid for the largest or
  smallest unit-level effect when effects vary (Caughey et al., 2023), but it
  is then not an interval for the average effect.

## Several outcomes: nonparametric combination

With more than one outcome, `npc()` tests each outcome separately using the same
relabellings, turns the results into p-values for every relabelling, and
combines them. The global p-value is the fraction of relabellings whose combined
value is at least the observed one.

```{r npc-data}
set.seed(2026)
z1 <- rnorm(20)
z2 <- 0.5 * z1 + sqrt(0.75) * rnorm(20)
dat <- data.frame(group = rep(c(1, 0), each = 10),
                  y1 = z1 + rep(c(0.8, 0), each = 10),
                  y2 = z2 + rep(c(0.5, 0), each = 10))
```

`shift` takes one value per outcome, or a single value that is used for every
outcome (with a message saying so). The default, `shift = 0`, tests no effect on
any outcome. A `shift` of any other length is an error.

```{r npc}
res <- npc(dat, group_col = "group", outcome_cols = c("y1", "y2"),
           alternative = "greater", shift = c(0, 0),
           combn = "tippett", reps = 10^3, seed = 1)
res$omnibus_p
dim(res$perm_set)
```

`npc()` returns a list with the global p-value (`omnibus_p`) and the
relabellings it used (`perm_set`). The default combining function is Fisher's.
The built-in combining functions are:

| `combn` | Value for component p-values $p_j$ | Large means evidence against the null |
|---|---|---|
| `"tippett"` | $\max_j (1 - p_j)$ | yes |
| `"fisher"` | $-2 \sum_j \log p_j$ | yes |
| `"liptak"` | $\sum_j \Phi^{-1}(1 - p_j)$ | yes |

Passing `perm_set = res$perm_set` makes the next call use the same relabellings,
so the combining functions can be compared on identical draws.

```{r npc-compare}
sapply(c("tippett", "fisher", "liptak"), function(cb)
  npc(dat, "group", c("y1", "y2"), alternative = "greater",
      shift = c(0, 0), combn = cb, perm_set = res$perm_set)$omnibus_p)
```

`combn` also accepts your own function of a vector of p-values. It must return a
number that is large when the evidence against the null is strong, so a sum of
p-values needs its sign reversed.

```{r npc-custom}
edgington <- function(p) -sum(p)
npc(dat, "group", c("y1", "y2"), alternative = "greater", shift = c(0, 0),
    combn = edgington, perm_set = res$perm_set)$omnibus_p
```

A shift other than zero tests a specific pair of effects:

```{r npc-shift}
npc(dat, "group", c("y1", "y2"), alternative = "greater",
    shift = c(0.8, 0.5), combn = "tippett",
    perm_set = res$perm_set)$omnibus_p
```

### How the global p-value is counted

For each outcome, the observed data and every relabelling get a partial p-value
from the permutation distribution, in the direction set by `alternative`. The
combining function turns each one's partial p-values into a single value. The
global p-value is the share of the `reps + 1` labellings (the observed one and
each relabelling) whose combined value is at least the observed one.

## Confidence regions for two outcomes

A confidence region for the pair of effects is the set of shifts
$(\eta_1, \eta_2)$ that the global test does not reject at level $\alpha$.
`npc_many()` evaluates the global p-value at each row of a grid of shifts, using
one set of relabellings throughout.

```{r npc-many}
grid <- expand.grid(eta1 = seq(-1.5, 2, length.out = 9),
                    eta2 = seq(-1.5, 2, length.out = 9))

many <- npc_many(df = dat, group_col = "group",
                 outcome_cols = c("y1", "y2"),
                 alternative = "greater",
                 param_values = grid,
                 test_stat = "diff_in_means",
                 combn = "tippett",
                 perm_set = res$perm_set)

head(many$global_p_values)
```

The result is a list. `global_p_values` is a matrix with columns `param1`,
`param2` and `global_p_value`, one row per grid point. `perm_set` is the set of
relabellings used. Each grid point is a separate call to `npc()`, so cost grows
with the grid size times the number of relabellings. Start with a coarse grid
and a modest `reps`.

```{r region, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4.5}
p <- matrix(many$global_p_values[, "global_p_value"], nrow = 9)
image(unique(grid$eta1), unique(grid$eta2), 1 * (p > 0.05),
      col = c("grey85", "steelblue"),
      xlab = expression(eta[1]), ylab = expression(eta[2]),
      main = "Shifts not rejected at level 0.05")
points(mean(dat$y1[dat$group == 1]) - mean(dat$y1[dat$group == 0]),
       mean(dat$y2[dat$group == 1]) - mean(dat$y2[dat$group == 0]),
       pch = 4, lwd = 2)
```

Three points to keep in mind when reading a region like this:

* **The global p-value is not monotone in the shifts.** Unlike the one-outcome
  case, the accepted region can have indents and narrow strips along its edges.
* **A grid is an approximation.** The p-value is a step function, so a grid can
  step over a change, and a feature narrower than the grid spacing can be
  missed. The region is not guaranteed to be conservative.
* **The alternative is one-sided here.** With `alternative = "greater"` the
  region has lower limits only and runs off the top and right of the plot.
  `"less"` gives upper limits, and `"two-sided"` gives a bounded region.

## Adjusting for multiple testing

```{r adjust}
pvals <- c(0.01, 0.04, 0.03, 0.20)
adjust_p_value(pvals, method = "holm-bonferroni")
adjust_p_value(pvals, method = "bonferroni")
adjust_p_value(pvals, method = "benjamini-hochberg")
```

## Practical notes

* **Choosing `reps`.** The p-value resolution is about $1/(\text{reps}+1)$. Use at
  least $10^4$ for a single test and more near the threshold. When the number of
  distinct assignments is small, enumerate them and, in `permutation_test()`, set
  `complete_enum = TRUE` for exact p-values.
* **Reproducibility.** Set `seed`, or fix the relabellings once with `perm_set`.
* **Validity.** The tests are valid for the randomization actually used, so
  `perm_func` has to match the assignment mechanism.

## References

Glazer, A. K. and Stark, P. B. (2024). Fast conservative Monte Carlo confidence
sets. arXiv:2405.05238. Published in the *Journal of Computational and
Graphical Statistics*, 2026.

Pesarin, F. and Salmaso, L. *Permutation Tests for Complex Data*. Wiley.

Caughey, D., Dafoe, A., Li, X. and Miratrix, L. (2023). Randomisation
inference beyond the sharp null. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society,
Series B*, 85, 1471-1491.
